cards.front: What makes an interstate a controlled-access road?
cards.back: Interstates are controlled-access roads with no stop signs, railroad crossings or traffic lights, and drivers get on and off only at interchanges without crossing other traffic.

cards.front: What risk have interstates and divided highways largely eliminated?
cards.back: Interstates and divided highways have largely eliminated the risk of head-on collisions, and they usually have few steep hills or sharp curves.

cards.front: What should you plan and check before an interstate trip?
cards.back: Plan your entrance, direction and exit ahead of time, and check your fuel first, since rural exits can be many miles apart.

cards.front: What should you do if you cannot drive at least the interstate minimum?
cards.back: If you cannot or do not want to drive at least the minimum speed, do not use the interstate.

cards.front: How do you enter an interstate?
cards.back: Unlike entering most busy roads, entering an interstate means speeding up: use the acceleration lane to reach traffic speed, signal left and merge when the way is clear.

cards.front: Who must yield when entering an interstate?
cards.back: The entering driver must yield the right-of-way to vehicles already on the interstate.

cards.front: What should drivers already on the interstate do for entering vehicles?
cards.back: Drivers already on the interstate should, for their own safety, make room for vehicles trying to enter, even though the entering driver must yield.

cards.front: What should you do if you must wait for a gap on an on-ramp?
cards.back: Do not stop at the end of an on-ramp; if you must wait for a gap, slow down on the ramp so you still have room to build speed, because stopping invites rear-end crashes.
cards.memory_hook: Slow on the ramp, never stop

cards.front: What does a lane added sign mean?
cards.back: A lane added sign means the ramp becomes a new lane so entering traffic need not merge at once, and through drivers should avoid moving right there.

cards.front: What does a merge sign mean?
cards.back: A merge sign means traffic from the right must merge into the existing right lane, so drivers already on the interstate should watch for it.

cards.front: What do trucks and buses joining the interstate need?
cards.back: Trucks and buses joining the interstate may need extra time and space to fit into traffic, so give it to them.

cards.front: Which lane should you leave for faster traffic on a multi-lane interstate?
cards.back: On multi-lane interstates, leave the far left lane for faster traffic, and do not ride alongside other vehicles where you sit in their blind spots.

cards.front: Why is lane-hopping a bad idea?
cards.back: Driving at an even speed reduces the need to change lanes, and lane-hopping raises crash risk, feeds road rage and rarely saves real time.

cards.front: Why avoid traveling in packs of cars?
cards.back: Avoid traveling in packs of cars and keep a space cushion around you for emergency moves.

cards.front: How far behind the vehicle ahead should you stay on the interstate?
cards.back: On the interstate stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead, and at least four seconds in bad weather, at night and on higher-speed rural stretches.

cards.front: What does following too closely cause on interstates?
cards.back: Following too closely causes many multiple-car crashes, and higher interstate speeds call for longer gaps.

cards.front: How far ahead should you scan on the interstate?
cards.back: Scan about fifteen to twenty seconds ahead for vehicles braking, entering or leaving.

cards.front: What should you do if traffic ahead slows or stops?
cards.back: If traffic ahead slows or stops, tap your brake pedal lightly several times to warn the drivers behind you.

cards.front: How should you keep pace with interstate traffic?
cards.back: Keep pace with traffic but never exceed the posted limit to stay with the flow, and if you drive slower than the flow, use the right lane.

cards.front: Why is driving too slowly on an interstate illegal?
cards.back: Driving too slowly on an interstate is illegal because it is as dangerous as speeding.

cards.front: What is the left lane for, and what should you do if a faster driver comes up behind you?
cards.back: The left lane is for passing only; if a faster driver comes up behind you there, move one lane to the right.

cards.front: Which drivers should be ready to move over so faster traffic can pass?
cards.back: Drivers in every lane except the right-hand slow lane should be ready to move over so faster traffic can pass.

cards.front: Who may use the HOV lane during peak hours?
cards.back: During the morning peak of seven to nine a.m. and the evening peak of four to six p.m., the HOV lane is reserved for vehicles with two or more people, motorcycles, buses and emergency vehicles.

cards.front: Does a baby count for the HOV lane, and may a single driver use it to pass?
cards.back: A baby in a car seat counts as a passenger for the HOV lane, and a single driver may not use it during peak hours even to pass.

cards.front: How does the HOV lane work outside peak hours, and what is the fine for a violation?
cards.back: Outside peak weekday hours and on weekends, the HOV lane works as an ordinary lane, and an HOV violation brings a fifty dollars fine plus court costs.

cards.front: How do you get into an HOV lane?
cards.back: HOV lanes sit at the far inside of the interstate, so to use one you merge onto the highway normally and then move across to the far inside lane.

cards.front: How many occupants do a bus and a motorcycle need for the HOV lane?
cards.back: Buses need two or more occupants to use the HOV lane at peak hours, while a motorcycle qualifies with just its rider.

cards.front: What must you do if you plan to exit before the HOV lane ends?
cards.back: If you plan to exit before the HOV lane ends, you must carefully move back across to the exit lane.

cards.front: When should you move to the right lane to exit?
cards.back: Move to the right lane early when you plan to exit, to avoid last-second lane changes.

cards.front: How far ahead do exit signs usually appear?
cards.back: Exit signs usually appear at least one mile before the exit, and in heavier traffic you should get into the exit lane sooner.

cards.front: When should you slow down to exit?
cards.back: Keep your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the ramp's posted speed and on to the limit of the road you are joining.

cards.front: What usually outlines the deceleration lane at an exit?
cards.back: The deceleration lane at an exit is usually outlined by a row of white reflectors.

cards.front: When may you drive on the interstate's paved shoulder?
cards.back: Do not drive on the interstate's paved shoulder except where marked for slowing down or in an emergency.

cards.front: May you park on an entrance or exit ramp?
cards.back: Parking on any part of an entrance or exit ramp is illegal unless the vehicle is disabled.

cards.front: At a diamond interchange, where is the exit ramp?
cards.back: At a diamond interchange the exit ramp always comes before you pass over or under the cross road, and you then obey its sign or signal and turn as at any intersection.

cards.front: From the cross road at a diamond interchange, where are the right-turn and left-turn ramps?
cards.back: From the cross road at a diamond interchange, the right-turn entrance ramp comes before you cross the interstate and the left-turn ramp after it, never the other way around.

cards.front: How do you turn left at a cloverleaf interchange?
cards.back: At a cloverleaf interchange every turn is a right turn: to go left, take the right-hand ramp just after the overpass.

cards.front: How do you turn right at a cloverleaf?
cards.back: At a cloverleaf, turning right means taking the right-hand ramp before the overpass, and the loop for a left turn leaves you heading as if you had turned left.

cards.front: What is a cloverleaf's advantage?
cards.back: A cloverleaf's advantage is that no turn crosses the path of other traffic.

cards.front: Why are weaving interchanges hazardous?
cards.back: A weaving interchange, where entering and exiting traffic share one lane, is among the most hazardous spots and calls for give-and-take from every driver.

cards.front: What should you expect at a weaving interchange?
cards.back: At a weaving interchange, expect drivers already on the interstate to move right toward the exit while you move left to enter, and both must yield and share.

cards.front: What should you do if you miss your interstate exit?
cards.back: Backing up, making a U-turn or crossing the median on an interstate is illegal; if you miss your exit, go on to the next one.

cards.front: Where may left turns and U-turns be made on the interstate?
cards.back: Left turns and U-turns on the interstate are allowed only through an opening provided and marked for them, and only emergency and maintenance crews may cross the median.

cards.front: What else may you not do on the interstate?
cards.back: On the interstate you may not change lanes without signaling, drive in another driver's blind spot, or get on except through a provided entrance.

cards.front: Where may you stop or park on the interstate?
cards.back: Stopping or parking on the interstate is allowed only in areas provided for it, and parking on the shoulder only in an emergency.

cards.front: What are good interstate driving habits?
cards.back: Good interstate habits include signaling well ahead, checking mirrors often, keeping a safe following distance and checking your speed and fuel gauges often.

cards.front: What hazards should you watch for on the interstate?
cards.back: Watch for pedestrians from broken-down vehicles, animals on the road and drivers going the wrong way.

cards.front: What do Dynamic Message Signs show?
cards.back: Dynamic Message Signs on urban Tennessee interstates, part of TDOT's SmartWay system, show real-time crash, weather and construction news, travel times and Amber Alerts, and are blank when not in use.

cards.front: Why is night driving more dangerous per mile?
cards.back: Night driving is far more dangerous per mile than daytime driving, mainly because of fatigue and poor vision, and drinking drivers are more often out at night.

cards.front: What is interstate hypnosis?
cards.back: Interstate hypnosis is drowsiness or unawareness brought on by long monotonous driving and the steady sound of wind, engine and tires.

cards.front: How can you fight interstate hypnosis?
cards.back: To fight interstate hypnosis, keep your eyes moving, keep the car cool, and stop as soon as you feel drowsy, since drowsiness is the first step to falling asleep.

cards.front: How often should you stop for a rest on long trips?
cards.back: Stop and step out of the car for a rest at least every two hours or about every one hundred miles, and avoid driving more than eight hours a day.
cards.memory_hook: Two hours or a hundred miles

cards.front: Which driver habits cause crashes and congestion?
cards.back: Rubbernecking, tailgating, needless lane changes and inattention all cause crashes and add to congestion.

cards.front: How can vehicles cause bottlenecks?
cards.back: Vehicles that run out of gas or break down from poor maintenance can cause bottlenecks, so watch your fuel and maintain your car.

cards.front: What does the Move Over Law require?
cards.back: The Move Over Law requires you to leave an empty lane next to a stopped emergency, utility, maintenance or recovery vehicle with flashing lights on an interstate or other highway with two or more lanes your way.

cards.front: Does moving over apply to either shoulder, and when may you just slow down?
cards.back: Moving over applies whichever shoulder the vehicle is on, and you may simply slow down in your lane only when a lane change would be unsafe.

cards.front: Which lane should you move into when the stopped vehicle is on the right shoulder?
cards.back: When the stopped vehicle is on the right shoulder, move into the left lane; when it is on the left shoulder, move into the right lane, leaving the nearest lane empty.

cards.front: Does the Move Over rule cover ordinary cars with flashing lights?
cards.back: The Move Over rule also covers any stopped vehicle on the shoulder, emergency lane or median that is showing flashing lights, including ordinary cars and trucks.

cards.front: Which vehicles does the Move Over Law cover?
cards.back: The Move Over Law covers police and Highway Patrol cars, ambulances and fire vehicles, utility and sanitation trucks, tow trucks, TDOT HELP and maintenance vehicles, and road contractors.

cards.front: What should you do when you have car trouble on the interstate?
cards.back: With car trouble, get onto the right shoulder or an emergency stopping area quickly and switch on your flashers.

cards.front: How should you signal for help after a breakdown?
cards.back: If your car breaks down and you need help, raise the hood and tie a white cloth to the hood or antenna, and if possible wait in or near the car on the side away from traffic.

cards.front: Why should you stay with your vehicle after a breakdown?
cards.back: Walking along the interstate is dangerous, so keep children away from traffic, and a passing officer not on another call will stop to help a driver who stays with the vehicle.

cards.front: In which cities may TDOT HELP trucks assist you?
cards.back: In Memphis, Nashville, Chattanooga and Knoxville, yellow TDOT HELP trucks may also assist stranded drivers.

cards.front: What authority do HELP operators have?
cards.back: HELP operators may remove any vehicle that obstructs or endangers traffic, and you must follow their directions as you would a police officer's.

cards.front: After a minor interstate crash, where may you move a drivable vehicle?
cards.back: After an interstate crash with no serious injuries or deaths, Tennessee law lets you move a drivable vehicle to the emergency lane to wait for police.
cards.memory_hook: Move it to the emergency lane

cards.front: At a crash scene, what must you do while waiting?
cards.back: While waiting at a crash scene you must stay, but you should not block traffic unnecessarily; TDOT signs remind drivers to move damaged vehicles to the shoulder when no one is seriously hurt.

cards.front: What must you never do at a crash scene?
cards.back: Never move a seriously injured person unless emergency personnel tell you to, never disturb a fatal crash scene, and never leave the scene of any crash.

cards.front: What should a roadside emergency kit include?
cards.back: A roadside kit should include a good spare tire, jack and tire iron, pressure gauge, flashlight with spare batteries, first aid kit, fire extinguisher, jumper cables, three reflectors or flares, insurance and registration papers, and a cell phone.

cards.front: What extra items should you carry in winter and summer?
cards.back: For winter trips also carry a blanket, a small portable heater, an ice scraper and snow tires or chains, and in summer carry bottled water.
cards.memory_hook: Blanket in winter, water in summer

recap_hooks.text: Speed up in the acceleration lane, yield to interstate traffic and never stop at the end of the ramp.
Stay at least two seconds back, four in harder conditions, and use the left lane only to pass.
At peak hours the HOV lane needs two or more people, and a single driver may not use it even to pass.
At a cloverleaf every turn is a right turn; to go left, take the ramp just after the overpass.
If you miss your exit, go on to the next one; never back up or cross the median.
Leave an empty lane next to a stopped vehicle with flashing lights, and slow down only if you cannot change lanes safely.
After a minor crash, move a drivable car to the emergency lane and stay at the scene.

merges.justification: sec10-F41 gives the Highway Patrol number to call at the crash scenes that sec10-F40 covers; its accepted wording carries a symbol that cannot be spoken as a card back, so the sec10-F40 card carries both.
